A technology project does not always slow down because the technology is difficult.
Sometimes, it slows down because the right expertise is not available when it is needed.
This is changing how organisations think about contract hiring.
Instead of using contract professionals only to fill temporary vacancies, businesses are increasingly bringing specialised talent into specific phases of a project.
For example:
• A Salesforce specialist for a CRM transformation
• Cloud engineers for a migration or modernisation project
• Data professionals for an analytics initiative
• AI specialists for a defined implementation
• Cybersecurity professionals for security and compliance projects
• ServiceNow experts for platform implementation and optimisation
The advantage is not simply adding more people.
It is adding the right expertise at the right stage of delivery.
This can help organisations:
• Accelerate project execution
• Address specialised skill gaps
• Reduce pressure on existing teams
• Scale resources around project demand
• Access expertise without permanently expanding every capability

A résumé rarely tells the full story of a Web3 builder.
In blockchain hiring, I’ve seen strong candidates whose real value is demonstrated through:
- GitHub contributions
- Smart contracts and protocols they’ve shipped
- DeFi/NFT products they’ve built
- Technical research and papers
- Open-source contributions
- Architecture and technical writing
- Demos and personal projects
- Community and ecosystem contributions
At the same time, someone can have a perfectly optimized résumé full of the right keywords without having actually built anything meaningful.
That’s why I think recruiting needs to move beyond “Does this CV match the job description?”
The better question is:
“What evidence shows this person can actually do the work?”
AI can help us process information faster, but hiring should ultimately be about understanding the *person behind the résumé* and the evidence of what they’ve accomplished.
This is particularly important in Web3, where a developer’s GitHub, protocol contributions, deployed contracts, research, and ecosystem involvement can tell us far more than a two-page CV.
Interesting direction from Lantern AI with Applicant Intelligence.
The future of recruiting shouldn’t be about better résumé optimization.
It should be about better talent discovery.

Every foreign company entering Saudi Arabia to set up their business assumes the city to do so is always Riyadh.

And for quite a few of them, perhaps.

But there are businesses for whom Riyadh is completely the wrong choice, and some find out six months and a significant investment too late.

>> Riyadh is the answer if you need to be close to power:

The capital is where government contracts get decided, where most of the Public Investment Fund (PIF) portfolio companies are headquartered, where the RHQ programme is concentrated, and where more than 675 international companies have already planted their flags. 

If your business model requires access to large corporate clients, government procurement, or the senior decision-makers driving Saudi Vision 2030, Riyadh is the right choice. 

>> Jeddah is the answer if your business is built on trade, tourism, or a more cosmopolitan consumer:

It's a port city, more open, more diverse in its social culture, and the natural gateway for businesses in logistics, hospitality, retail, and anything touching the holy cities. The consumer in Jeddah is different from the consumer in Riyadh, more internationally oriented, more experience-driven, and in some categories, more accessible for foreign brands in their early stages. 

If your revenue model depends on footfall, tourism, or trade flows rather than corporate contracts, Jeddah deserves serious consideration.

>> NEOM is the answer if you're building for a decade from now and your sector qualifies:

Zero corporate tax for 30 years, independent legal framework, and foreign ownership without a local partner in qualifying sectors. NEOM is really a great place for the right business, specifically technology, clean energy, AI, biotech, and advanced manufacturing. 

But the runway to revenue is longer, the operational requirements are real, and the ecosystem is still forming. If you need revenue in year one, NEOM is not the right starting point.

Choosing the right city when you’re coming to Saudi for setting up the business is something that you can’t get wrong because it shapes everything that follows, your legal structure, your hiring pool, your client access, and your ability to win the contracts you actually came here for.

Get this right before you get excited about anything else.

Boards and AI: 6 questions directors should ask before adopting AI

AI tools are already in many Nigerian workplaces. Staff use them to draft documents, screen CVs, answer customers and analyse data, often before anyone in leadership has set rules.

When something goes wrong, the questions come to the board.

You don't need to be technical to govern AI well. You need to ask good questions and expect clear answers. Here are six:

1. What exactly will it be used for?
"Using AI" is too vague. Is it a drafting helper, or is it influencing decisions about people or money?

2. What data goes into it?
Customer details, staff records and contracts can all end up in an AI tool. If personal data is involved, the NDPA applies.

3. Who is accountable for it?
AI doesn't carry responsibility. A named person should own each use, and the board should know who that is.

4. How is it checked for errors and bias?
AI can be wrong, and it can treat people unfairly, especially in hiring, lending and customer decisions. A human should review the results before they affect someone.

5. What do our vendor contracts say?
Who owns the data you put in? Can the provider reuse it? Where is it stored? Who is liable if something goes wrong?

6. Do we have a policy and a plan?
A short AI use policy tells staff what they can and cannot share. A simple incident plan says what to do if something goes wrong, including a data breach.

Adopting AI is a business decision. Governing it is the board's job.

Directors and business owners: does your leadership team have an AI use policy yet? Tell me in the comments. 👇

General information, not legal advice.

As I was writing my umpteenth lettre de motivation in French, I wondered: how much of what a candidate can do, gets lost under the rules of a language they have yet to fully perfect?

I'm Malaysian of Chinese Peranakan descent. I grew up between Malay, English, Mandarin and Hokkien, and picked up Indonesian and Cantonese along the way. For the past 12 years, I've been sharing a life with my French spouse. My daily life is a constant navigation across Hofstede's cultural dimensions: when to be direct and when to keep the harmony, when to have everything planned and when to let things unfold naturally, as Lao Tzu would have it.

I came to realise that speaking several languages is not only about communicating fluently with different interlocutors. Rather, it is also about interpreting an idea from different perspectives, and knowing how to convey it to different audiences. Once you have experienced that, you will look at a problem with multiple possibilities.

I'm of the opinion that this ability is more than a soft skill - it is a business advantage. I met a recruiter at the recent VivaTech 2026, who told me that they appreciate hiring Malaysians because of our multilingual and multicultural competencies. Multilinguals open doors to new markets and clients. They notice when the way of working in Paris will be counterproductive in Kuala Lumpur before it costs anything. They are the bridge between headquarters and local teams who would otherwise be talking past each other. A European Commission study of nearly 2,000 exporting SMEs found that 11% had lost a contract because of a lack of language skills. This shows that there is a cost of not having multilinguals.

Today, AI can polish anyone's cover letter in seconds, and that is a new problem in itself. LinkedIn's CEO recently said that recruiters are drowning in a sea of applications that look the same. What stands out now is a real perspective, shaped by real experiences. While I agree with this, I think of job seekers looking for opportunities away from home - so much can get lost in translation when we operate in a language that we are still learning.

I think as long as the hiring process is still heavily automated, the qualities a team needs most, might often not reach a human. What AI can do is translate our words, but it can't translate our judgement.

 💡 My wish for recruiters: Ask questions like 'What have you learned from living between cultures, and how will you apply that to your role?' in applications, on top of language proficiency. 
Or
before an application is screened out for imperfect French, give it one human read. What's missing in grammar may be more than made up for in perspective. 

 📢 To my fellow multilinguals, how many languages do you speak, and what challenges have you faced applying for jobs away from home?

2. Developers will be rehired to clean up the mess AI made.

We've seen this movie before.
Offshore outsourcing promised cheaper, faster software.
It delivered — and then companies spent years fixing the technical debt.

AI is following the exact same script.
Businesses will ship fast with AI-generated code.
Then one day the system breaks, nobody understands why, and they'll desperately need a senior engineer who actually knows what's happening under the hood.

The irony? The developers AI displaced will be the ones called back to fix it.

3. The AI bubble will burst.

Not all of it. But enough to hurt.
Valuations are disconnected from reality.
Half the "AI startups" are wrappers around GPT with a nice UI.
When revenue doesn't match the hype — and it won't for many — the correction will be brutal.

The companies built on real AI integration will survive and thrive.
The ones built on AI theatre will vanish overnight.


Here's what I actually believe though —
AI isn't the end of human work.
It's the end of lazy, replaceable, low-skill work.

The developers who survive and thrive will be the ones who:
→ Understand systems deeply, not just syntax
→ Use AI as a force multiplier, not a crutch
→ Can clean up what AI gets wrong — and know why it got it wrong


I've been building with AI in production for years.
Not as a shortcut. As a multiplier.

The bubble may burst. The mess will need cleaning.
I'll still be here — building, leading and shipping.

Every company in India deploying an LLM now has a legal problem it has not priced.

The problem is not whether the model is good. The problem is what happens when it is wrong. A customer is misled. A loan is denied. A hiring decision is biased. A data subject's rights are ignored. A regulator asks a question the company cannot answer.

The lawyers inside these companies do not know what a context window is. The engineers do not know what the DPDPA requires. The gap between the two is where the liability sits.

The Advocacy — A Law Firm exists to close that gap.

Our focus is corporate litigation, insolvency and restructuring, and arbitration. Over the past year we have built a second practice area: data protection and AI governance.

The DPDPA compliance deadline is 13 May 2027. Full obligations take effect on that date. The Data Protection Board will begin adjudicating. Most Indian companies have not started.

We have built a retrieval-first legal engine called Unknown Verdict. It returns the verbatim text of an Indian statute, cited to the source PDF and page number. No generation in the retrieval path. No marginal cost per query. It is live at https://lnkd.in/dX8wBcvw, and published under our Article 39A commitment to equal access to justice.

We have authored a working paper titled Calculator, Not Mind: Anthropomorphic Language and the Risk of a Liability Shield for AI Developers. The paper argues that mental predicates applied to language models — "thinking," "reasoning," "refusing," "acting autonomously" — shift responsibility from the company that built the system to the tool itself. It is under review by legal practitioners before publication.

Services

We offer four defined engagements. Not hours. Deliverables.

AI Liability Audit. For companies deploying any AI system. A written report identifying where the company is exposed if the system produces a wrong output, who the legal doer is under current law, and what mitigations are required. Fixed fee.

DPDPA Readiness Assessment. A gap assessment across data processing, notice, consent, breach response, and Data Processing Agreements. Prioritised remediation plan with cost and timeline. Fixed fee.

DPO-as-a-Service. An outsourced Data Protection Officer for companies that require one but do not need a full-time hire. Monthly retainer. Recurring.

AI Governance Programme. For companies with multiple AI systems across jurisdictions. Ongoing policy stack review, contract drafting, incident response, board-level training. Monthly retainer.

We also provide fractional General Counsel support.


Our advisory work, our tools, and our research exist to remove that shield.

If your company is deploying AI, or processing personal data, and has not yet assessed its exposure, we should talk. The deadline is seven months away.

HR doesn't have the time to complete a lengthy spreadsheet, and Privacy doesn't have the bandwidth to chase responses over email for three weeks.

🔹 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 & 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴

The objective isn't simply to say “No.”

48% of US hiring managers would rather invest in AI tools than hire and train a recent grad.

I'm a recent grad. Fun read.

But the same survey says something else.

65% still plan to hire the same number of 2026 grads, or more.

Both can be true.

My read: entry-level jobs aren't vanishing. The bar for "entry-level" is moving.

Look at the other numbers:

→ 61% would only consider grads without an internship for certain roles, or not at all
→ 76% said new grads need help with basic documents like memos and contracts

Nobody is asking for more theory.

They're asking for proof you can do the work.

And honestly, this is where "entry-level" gets confusing.

If companies expect graduates to arrive with internships, projects and workplace experience, what exactly counts as entry-level anymore?

A degree says I can learn.

A project says I can do.

That's why I'm trying to build both.

Fewer jobs isn't the whole story. A higher bar is.
